directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; True Zebra Haworthia is genuinely rare in cultivation, since most plants sold under this name are actually the far more common Haworthiopsis attenuata. The two are easy to tell apart once you know the trick: this species carries its raised white tubercle bands only on the outer, convex face of each leaf, leaving the inner face smooth and glossy, while H. attenuata is banded on both surfaces. Leaves are also narrower, thicker, and curve inward more sharply, giving the rosette a tighter, more bulbous outline than its common look-alike. It slowly clusters into a small colony via offsets, making it a good candidate for a shallow collector's dish alongside other true-species haworthias.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Cobweb Aloe's fine leaf-edge bristles trap tiny amounts of moisture and reflect harsh light, so avoid the intense midday sun that would scorch its more open rosette.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Cobweb Aloe's fine leaf-edge bristles trap tiny amounts of moisture and reflect harsh light, so avoid the intense midday sun that would scorch its more open rosette. Unlike the tightly packed, window-topped rosettes of Haworthia cooperi or H. pumila already common in collections, this species has slender, pointed, dark green to brownish leaves fringed with soft white filaments that give the whole plant a cobwebbed appearance, an adaptation that shades the leaf surface in its exposed rocky habitat. Rosettes stay small and eventually clump slowly outward, and mature plants send up thin, wiry flower spikes bearing small whitish blooms in spring. Native to rock crevices across South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape, it tolerates the same low-water, high-drainage regimen as other small haworthias and is easily separated by offset for propagation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant in full sun in gritty, low-fertility, very well-drained soil; this species flowers on a different schedule than most desert roses, blooming heaviest from late summer into early winter rather than in a single spring flush.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, low-fertility, very well-drained soil; this species flowers on a different schedule than most desert roses, blooming heaviest from late summer into early winter rather than in a single spring flush. It closely resembles Adenium swazicum but grows with more upright, woody stems rather than a lax, sprawling habit, and carries much broader, rounder leaves along with smaller, more solidly colored pink flowers that lack the contrasting pale throat seen in many other Adenium species. Native to the arid escarpment of northern Namibia and southern Angola, it forms a modest, swollen caudex at the base of its stems rather than the huge bottle-shaped trunk of A. arabicum or A. socotranum. Reduce watering and protect from any chill well before winter, since all plant parts contain toxic sap and it has no frost tolerance whatsoever.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in full sun in a shallow, wide container with gritty, very well-drained soil; this is the smallest and slowest Adenium species, so expect years rather than months between visible growth stages.

directions: Plant in full sun in a shallow, wide container with gritty, very well-drained soil; this is the smallest and slowest Adenium species, so expect years rather than months between visible growth stages. Instead of the tall bottle-shaped trunk of A. arabicum or A. socotranum, it forms a thick, mostly subterranean tuberous root that stays largely buried, sending up only a few thin, weak stems with narrow leaves above the soil line. Small, uniform pink flowers appear sparingly, and the plant observes a long winter dormancy during which it may drop its leaves entirely and should be kept nearly dry. Native to the dry sandveld of northern South Africa and Botswana, it is best displayed with the upper caudex partially exposed, bonsai-style, to show off its odd, root-like form.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in full sun in gritty, very well-drained soil; kept warm and watered through the year, Somali Desert Rose will stay in leaf almost continuously rather than dropping foliage for a hard winter dormancy.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, very well-drained soil; kept warm and watered through the year, Somali Desert Rose will stay in leaf almost continuously rather than dropping foliage for a hard winter dormancy like many of its relatives. Twisting, swollen stems and narrow, blade-like leaves give it a more sculptural, gnarled silhouette than the rounder-leaved A. obesum, and its trumpet-shaped flowers range more widely in color, from pink to white to deep crimson-red, depending on the population. Native to the arid Horn of Africa and East African coast, it can eventually become tree-like in habitat, though container specimens stay far more compact. Protect it from any cold and reduce water if temperatures drop, since it has no frost tolerance and all parts of the plant contain toxic sap.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in full sun in coarse, sandy, extremely well-drained soil; unlike the Madagascar pachypodiums that want to be kept bone-dry in winter, Halfmens comes from a winter-rainfall region and appreciates occasional water during the cooler months.

directions: Plant in full sun in coarse, sandy, extremely well-drained soil; unlike the Madagascar pachypodiums that want to be kept bone-dry in winter, Halfmens comes from a winter-rainfall region and appreciates occasional water during the cooler months. It grows as a single, rarely branching, spine-covered column topped with a dense rosette of velvety gray-green leaves, and in habitat it characteristically leans toward the equator as it ages, giving rise to its Afrikaans name meaning 'half-human.' This unbranched, top-heavy growth habit sets it apart from the multi-branched Pachypodium saundersii or the flat, clustering Pachypodium brevicaule already in cultivation, and it is far slower to reach flowering size than the Madagascar tree species. Native to the rocky Richtersveld and Namaqualand region straddling South Africa and Namibia, it is toxic if ingested and should be handled carefully when repotting the young, spine-covered stem.
sources: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in full sun in a shallow, wide pot with coarse, mineral, extremely well-drained soil; this is the slowest-growing and most compact Pachypodium species, so choose a container that fits its flattened shape rather than its eventual size.

directions: Plant in full sun in a shallow, wide pot with coarse, mineral, extremely well-drained soil; this is the slowest-growing and most compact Pachypodium species, so choose a container that fits its flattened shape rather than its eventual size. Rather than the tall bottle or tree forms of P. lamerei, P. geayi, or P. rosulatum, it develops as a low, wide, gray caudex studded with short spine clusters and small leafy branch nubs, giving mature plants an odd, flattened, almost molten look rarely taller than a few inches despite a diameter of a foot or more. Bright yellow flowers are borne close against the caudex surface in summer rather than on tall stalks. Native to quartzite and sandstone outcrops in central Madagascar, it is a favorite collector's plant precisely because of its bizarre, slow-motion sculptural form, and it should be watered generously in summer growth but kept dry during its winter leaf-drop dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, shielding it from harsh midday summer sun that can scorch its thick, water-filled leaves.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, shielding it from harsh midday summer sun that can scorch its thick, water-filled leaves. Its large, scalloped, blue-green leaves are much bigger and softer-edged than the narrow, pencil-like leaves of Kalanchoe daigremontiana or K. delagoensis, and readily sprout tiny plantlets along the notches of the leaf margin wherever a leaf touches soil, even after being detached from the plant entirely. Clusters of pendant, greenish-pink, bell-shaped flowers appear on tall stalks in winter above the foliage. Long used across the tropics as a folk remedy earning it the names Miracle Leaf and Life Plant, it self-sows aggressively from fallen leaves in warm climates, so grow it in a container if unchecked spread is a concern.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; contain this plant carefully, since the tiny plantlets that form at each leaf tip root readily and it self-sows aggressively, becoming weedy or even toxic to grazing animals in warm climates.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; contain this plant carefully, since the tiny plantlets that form at each leaf tip root readily and it self-sows aggressively, becoming weedy or even toxic to grazing animals in warm climates. Its slender, cylindrical, pencil-like leaves mottled with purplish-brown blotches are quite different from the flat, broad, triangular leaves of Kalanchoe daigremontiana, and its plantlets cluster only at the notched leaf tips rather than all along the margin. Clusters of dangling, tubular, orange-red flowers open atop upright stems in winter, adding color when little else in the succulent collection is blooming. Native to Madagascar and long naturalized in warm regions worldwide, it is best grown in a contained pot set where dropped plantlets cannot easily root in surrounding garden soil.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
